A high school student discovered a comet using publicly available NASA spacecraft images, turning a school project into an astronomy career and major scientific recognition.

Finding a new comet was once a pursuit largely limited to professional astronomers and a small number of experienced amateur skywatchers with access to telescopes. The rise of online spacecraft data has changed that, allowing people with little more than a computer, an internet connection and patience to search for objects that can be difficult or impossible to spot from Earth.

One of the clearest examples is planetary astronomer Quanzhi Ye, who discovered a tiny sungrazing comet in 2005 while he was still in high school. Ye was examining publicly available images from the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO), a joint European Space Agency and NASA mission, through the NASA-funded Sungrazer citizen science project. His discovery became the project's 1,019th comet and was followed by several more comet discoveries from the same platform.

The achievement eventually became the starting point for an astronomy career. Ye went on to study planetary science and astronomy and, in 2023, received the Harold C. Urey Prize from the American Astronomical Society's Division for Planetary Sciences for his early-career work on small bodies in the solar system.

How the Sungrazer Project lets people hunt for comets

SOHO was launched in 1995 and began returning images that revealed objects close to the Sun. Its Large Angle Spectrometric Coronagraph, or LASCO, uses an occulting disc to block the Sun's intense glare, making the surrounding region visible to its cameras. That has allowed scientists and members of the public to spot faint comets passing close to the Sun.

The mission was not designed specifically as a comet-hunting spacecraft. However, people examining its images began reporting previously unidentified objects, eventually leading to the creation of the Sungrazer Project. The NASA-funded citizen science programme gives volunteers around the world access to spacecraft images and allows them to report suspected new sungrazing and near-Sun comets.

These objects can be extremely difficult to observe using conventional telescopes. Many sungrazing comets pass so close to the Sun that they break apart or are destroyed, while their faintness makes them difficult to detect from the ground. Space-based coronagraph images therefore provide an unusual opportunity to study them.

The scale of the project has grown dramatically. In March 2024, SOHO reached its 5,000th comet discovery, with citizen scientist Hanjie Tan spotting the object in SOHO data. Tan had been participating in the Sungrazer Project since he was 13. NASA and the US Naval Research Laboratory said the milestone demonstrated the major contribution made by volunteers to comet research.

Quanzhi Ye's journey from comet hunter to astronomer

Ye's first discovery came in 2005, when he was a high school student. According to NASA, the comet was identified in images from SOHO's LASCO C3 telescope and became the 1,019th comet reported through the Sungrazer Project. It was the first of several discoveries Ye would make through the programme.

Rather than remaining a one-off school achievement, the experience became an early step towards a professional research career. Ye earned a Bachelor of Science degree from Sun Yat-Sen University in China before completing a master's degree and Ph.D. in astronomy at the University of Western Ontario in Canada. He later undertook postdoctoral research at the California Institute of Technology.

His research has focused on small bodies in the solar system, including the relationships between comets, asteroids and meteoroids. His work has also examined meteor showers, interstellar comets and near-Earth asteroids.

In 2023, the Division for Planetary Sciences of the American Astronomical Society awarded Ye the Harold C. Urey Prize. The award recognises outstanding achievements in planetary science by an early-career scientist. The citation highlighted his contributions to understanding small bodies in the inner solar system, including research linking meteor showers to specific comets and asteroids.

From public space data to real scientific discoveries

The Sungrazer Project has since developed into a major citizen science effort, with thousands of comet discoveries attributed to participants. NASA describes it as a research effort in which volunteers can use spacecraft data to search for new comets without needing professional astronomical equipment.

The project also illustrates how publicly accessible scientific data can open opportunities beyond traditional observatories and research institutions. A teenager examining images on a computer was able to make a genuine contribution to planetary science, and that early experience eventually developed into a professional research career.

SOHO's success has also shown that scientific discoveries can emerge from data collected for a broader purpose. By making spacecraft observations available to citizen scientists, missions such as SOHO have allowed people outside professional astronomy to participate directly in the search for objects moving through the inner solar system.
